critique.good: The row-label column is the widest of the three (81px), and all five month columns are identical in width, so the time series still reads as one comparable unit. Headers stay on one line and no value overflows.
critique.problems: The month columns look pinched: the 4-digit numbers sit almost flush against the cell borders, noticeably tighter than the header text above them, and the numbers have less air than in r0B or r0C. Meanwhile the extra width given to 门店 buys nothing visible — the store names still break after three characters, so the column is wider without being better. The result is an unbalanced budget: width was taken from the columns that must stay legible (the numbers) and handed to the column that cannot use it.
critique.cause: Month widths of 55px leave only 34px of text space for content that needs 35px — below the safe minimum. Col 1 at 81px yields 60px of text space, which is exactly 4 characters at 15px, so in practice it rounds under and still fits only 3 characters; 4-character lines would need roughly 82–84px, which the 360px budget cannot afford alongside five usable month columns.

critique.good: The best balance of the three. Month columns at 57px give 36px of text space — 1px of slack over the 35px requirement — so every 4-digit value and every 1月–5月 header sits clear of the borders while all five months stay exactly equal. Col 1 at 74px gives 53px of text space, comfortably fitting three characters (45px) with ~8px of breathing room, so names break 3+2 or 3+3 without a lone orphan character on the second line. Rows read as coherent units.
critique.problems: No structural fault. Only the inherent consequence of the budget: every store name occupies two lines, and the shorter second line (汇店, 店) makes the label column look slightly ragged. Nothing here is caused by a bad width choice.
critique.cause: 74px row-label column is the largest value that still allows 57px month columns (74 + 5×57 = 359), and 57px is the smallest month width that gives visible slack around the numbers.

critique.good: The month columns get the most air of the three (58px → 37px of text space), so the numeric grid is the calmest and the vertical scan across months is easiest. Month widths are equal, headers unwrapped, table fits at 359px.
critique.problems: The row-label column is now over-compressed: store names crowd the left and right borders and the 门店 column stops reading as a distinct anchor that introduces each row — it looks like just another narrow column. The gain in the month columns is only 1px over r0B, so the trade is poor value: it sacrifices the anchor to buy an invisible improvement.
critique.cause: Col 1 at 68px leaves 47px of text space for three characters that need 45px — only 2px of slack, which is why the names look wedged against the cell edges.

critique.good: The five month columns are equal at 57px, so every 4-digit value has 36px of content space and sits comfortably on one line; headers stay unwrapped and vertical comparison across stores is clean.
critique.problems: 门店 is the tightest element: its 53px text box makes the first line of every store name nearly touch the cell edge, so the row labels look squeezed against the numbers. The 1px surplus in each month column buys nothing because 35px already fits the values. The table reads as a numeric grid with a cramped label strip rather than rows anchored by readable labels.
critique.cause: col1=74 leaves only 53px for text, far below the 92px one-line need. The 5px removed from the label is spread across five 57px month columns, giving 36px content where 35px is sufficient.

critique.good: All headers and numbers fit without wrapping, truncation, or overflow; the five month columns are equal, so scanning a single month down the stores is straightforward.
critique.problems: This is the most imbalanced version: the 48px label measure is visibly starved, with 3-character lines almost touching both edges and a large ragged gap after the 2-character second line. Meanwhile each month column has 37px content, 2px more than needed, so the numeric area is loose while the labels are cramped. The eye notices the tight label column first.
critique.cause: col1=69 yields 48px text; months=58 yield 37px content. The 10px shifted from the label to the month columns does not change any line break, because 3 Chinese characters still fit and 4 still do not, so it only worsens proportion.

critique.good: Best balance of the three: 门店 gets the maximum 79px, or 58px of text, possible while the five month columns remain equal at the 56px minimum. Each month has exactly 35px content for the 4-digit values, the label column has breathing room, and the table reads row-first as intended.
critique.problems: Store names still wrap to two lines; 5-character names break 3+2 such as 上海徐 / 汇店, leaving a short second line, and 6-character names break 3+3. This is unavoidable at 58px: 3 Chinese characters fit, while 4 need about 60px. Pushing col1 to 81px would fit 4 characters but create a 4+1 single-character orphan for the five 5-character names, which is worse. The 60px row height and airy numeric cells follow from the mandatory two-line labels, not from a width error.
critique.cause: col1=79 gives 58px text, just under the 60px needed for 4 characters; months=56 give 35px content, exactly the longest number. This is the Pareto optimum under the 359px cap with equal month columns.

r0A.idea: Prioritize row labels: keep every month column at its one-line minimum and give 门店 the remaining 81px, so store names wrap at four characters.

r0B.idea: Balance both roles with a regular 57px month grid and a 74px row-label column, accepting slightly more wrapping in store names.

r0C.idea: Treat the five months as the dominant comparison grid: equal 58px columns give numbers more air, while 门店 shrinks to 68px and store names wrap at three characters.

r1A.idea: Confirms and locks in the r0B allocation as the reference: col 1 at 74px (53px text, ~8px slack for three characters, no orphan lines) and five equal 57px month columns (36px text, 1px slack over the 35px requirement). This is the widest anchor column that still permits month columns with real breathing room, so it fixes r0A's pinched numbers without r0C's cramped labels.

r1B.idea: Test the opposite bias from r0A: take 1px from the anchor and give it to all five months, so numbers get 37px of text space (2px slack) while col 1 still holds three characters per line (48px text vs 45px needed). Keeps month widths exactly equal; a compromise that favours numeric legibility while keeping the label column just wide enough to avoid border-hugging.

r1C.idea: New idea: push the row-label column to its practical maximum (79px → 58px text) and hold every month column at exactly 56px, the precise one-line minimum (35px text). This tests whether a stronger row anchor and maximal label breathing room is worth running the numeric columns at zero slack; months remain exactly equal, so comparability is preserved either way.

contrast.idea: A plausible 'balance the numbers' move that starves the label column to 25px of text: store names collapse into 3–4 short lines, rows stop reading as units, and the row heights grow while the digits sit in generous, useless whitespace.

understanding.purpose: Compare monthly sales across East China stores and reveal each store's month-to-month trend over January–May.
understanding.reading: Readers scan row by row to identify a store, then read left to right across the five months; they also compare a single month vertically across stores. The row-label column anchors each row, while the month columns form one continuous comparable series.
groups: Column 1 (门店): row-label column identifying each store.
Columns 2–6 (1月–5月): one comparable time series; keep near-equal widths and consistent alignment so month-to-month differences read cleanly.
keep_intact: All numeric sales values, with no wrapping, truncation, or overflow.
门店 header and the full characters of every store name; store names may wrap but must not be truncated.
may_wrap: Store names such as 上海徐汇店 and 南京新街口店 may wrap at Chinese character boundaries; row height can absorb two lines.
Month headers and numbers should not wrap.

bad.why: Width is misallocated: the row-identity column is squeezed to 68px (47px of text) so every 5–6 character store name breaks into a cramped 3+2/3+3 rag, while the five month columns — whose digits need only 35px — are padded to 58px. The eye starts at the store name; starving it to over-feed identical numeric columns inverts the table's hierarchy.

A plausible 'balance the numbers' move that starves the label column to 25px of text: store names collapse into 3–4 short lines, rows stop reading as units, and the row heights grow while the digits sit in generous, useless whitespace.

contrast.why: A plausible 'balance the numbers' move that starves the label column to 25px of text: store names collapse into 3–4 short lines, rows stop reading as units, and the row heights grow while the digits sit in generous, useless whitespace.

final.rationale: The table is one label column plus five identical repeated-measure numeric columns, so the label column should take all slack after the numbers get their minimum. One-line store names are impossible here (they would need ~113px against a 360px budget), so the real question is only how the 2-line rag and the surrounding whitespace read. r1C gives the store column the maximum the numbers can spare (79px) while keeping all five month columns identical at 56px — exactly enough for '1284' at 35px of text — so the repeated columns stay perfectly comparable and the identifier column is as strong as the grid allows. r0C/r1B spend width on digits that don't need it and leave the names visually pinched, which is the wrong direction of generosity.

general: Budget the row-label column first: give homogeneous numeric columns only longest-number-plus-slack, and route every remaining pixel to the column that carries words.
Columns that repeat the same measure (months, years, variants) should be exactly equal in width so digit positions line up and no column reads as more important.
In CJK tables characters break anywhere, so widening a label column often does not reduce line count — judge such widths by rag quality and whitespace balance, not by wrapping alone.
A 1px difference among numeric columns is invisible; never trade label-column width for that kind of nominal symmetry.
specific: At 360px, one-line store names (needing ~113px) are unattainable; 2-line names are the floor and every candidate already hits it.
Because 47–60px of text all fit three CJK characters per line, col 1 widths from ~68 to ~81 produce identical line breaks — the choice is purely about rag and proportion, not row height.
56px is the hard floor for the month columns (35px digit width + 21px padding/border); 58px is comfortable; beyond that is waste at this table size.

final.tradeoffs: A careful designer could argue for a little slack in the numeric columns (r1B at 58px) to protect against font-metric variation and keep digits off the cell edge, accepting a visibly tighter store column; others would rather spend those pixels on the label column as r1C does. Some would also find the 1–2px asymmetry in r0A/r1A harmless.
final.uncertain: Whether the 1px asymmetry in r0A is perceptible at all, and whether the exact-fit 55px month columns risk clipping under different font rendering. Also out of scope: whether this table should keep full grid rules or transpose months into rows, which would change the width problem entirely.

A.why: Column 1 gets about 72px, so all store names break 3+2 (上海徐/汇店, 南京新/街口店), cutting place names in half; the resulting two-line blocks are even and the five month columns stay equal and comfortably wide, so numbers scan cleanly, but the row headers are the weak point.

B.why: Effectively the same as A: identical 3+2 wrapping of store names (杭州西/湖店, 苏州观/前店), even two-line row blocks and even month columns; nothing broken, but row identity is split mid-place-name, which slows reading down the header column.

C.why: Same 3+2 name wrap as A and B; month columns look evenly proportioned and the numeric grid reads as a clean block, yet the header column still chops 徐汇, 西湖 and 新街口, so the row labels lose a little integrity.

D.why: The wider header column lets each name put city+district on line one (上海徐汇, 南京新街, 合肥淮河) and isolates the generic suffix 店 on line two, so the distinguishing part stays intact and the lone 店 forms a consistent vertical rhythm; the cost is slightly squeezed month columns (numbers sit closer to the rules) and a stranded single character per row, but the table scans better down the row headers.

E.why: The header column is so narrow that names break into three lines (上海/徐汇/店, 南京/新街/口店), producing very tall, airy rows; the whole table becomes a ladder of text with the month figures floating far apart, breaking row cohesion and vertical comparison between months.

F.why: Same 3+2 split as A/B/C with balanced month columns; readable and consistent, but the row-header breaks fall inside place names (宁波天/一店, 合肥淮/河路店), which is the weakest aspect of an otherwise tidy grid.

reviews.unsure: A, B, C and F look nearly identical in the renders, so I cannot tell whether their month-column widths differ by a pixel or two; my ranking of D over them rests on the name-wrap pattern rather than measurable width differences, and D sits right at the minimum month-column width (about 55px vs the 56px one-line need), which could pinch digits on a slightly different font.

A.why: 门店 column is only about three characters wide, so every store name splits mid-word (上海徐/汇店, 杭州西/湖店, 苏州观/前店, 宁波天/一店), breaking the branch names readers scan by. The month columns still have spare room that should have gone to column 1.

B.why: Best balance of the compact layouts: the wider row-header column keeps most branch names intact (上海徐汇/店, 杭州西湖/店), leaving only the trailing 店 orphaned, while all four-digit figures still sit on one line. A few bad splits remain (南京新街/口店), but the table stays compact and scannable.

C.why: Same failure as A: three-character header column cuts through branch names (徐/汇, 西/湖, 观/前, 天/一), so row identity is fragmented while the month columns carry unnecessary slack.

D.why: Row headers again wrap at three characters, splitting 徐汇, 西湖, 观前 and 天一 across lines; the month columns are wider than the numbers require, so the space is misallocated.

E.why: Visually the same compromise as A/C/D: row labels break inside branch names and the numeric columns keep extra width that column 1 needs more.

F.why: Two-character breaks give a readable city/branch rhythm (上海/徐汇/店, 苏州/观前/店), but 新街口 and 淮河路 still split badly (口店, 路店), and every row becomes three lines tall. The month columns are clearly over-wide for four-digit numbers, wasting width that could have kept column 1 to two or three clean lines.

reviews.unsure: A, C, D and E look nearly identical at this resolution, so small width differences may be invisible; also a judgment call whether F's semantic two-character breaks outweigh its extra row height and over-wide numeric columns.
